conventions.convention: Real estimators are measurable maps to the real Borel space. Bias requires integrability at the parameter considered; MSE is an extended nonnegative expectation and equals deterministic squared-error risk. No measurable structure on the parameter set is required.

Unbiasedness requires integrability and the correct expectation at every parameter. Finite-variance unbiasedness requires square-integrability at every parameter. UMVU compares against all other finite-variance unbiased estimators of the same estimand throughout the parameter space.

Rao–Blackwell assumes AC, standard-Borel data and statistic spaces, and a supplied parameter-independent common conditional-law kernel. Its Borel function g is common across parameters; conditional-expectation identities and variance equality conditions are interpreted separately almost surely under each parameter law.
Lehmann–Scheffé uniqueness means equality almost surely under each parameter law, rather than pointwise equality or an asserted common exceptional null set.
The Bernoulli sample has n ≥ 1 and p ∈ [0,1], including both degenerate endpoints.

The Rao–Blackwell Bernoulli example uses the finite discrete data space {0,1}^n and statistic space {0,…,n}, with n ≥ 1 and p ∈ [0,1]. The uniform kernel is defined on every fiber, including fibers unsupported by an endpoint law.
The biased constant estimator's improvement is pointwise at p = 1/5; it is not uniform over p ∈ [0,1].

load_bearing.statement: Assume AC, standard-Borel data and statistic spaces, and a sufficient statistic S with a supplied common parameter-independent conditional-law kernel. For a measurable real estimator U with Eθ[U] = ψ(θ) and Eθ[U²] < ∞ for every θ, there is a single Borel function g, independent of θ, such that g(S) is a version of Eθ[U | σ(S)] for every θ. It is unbiased, finite-variance, and Varθ(g(S)) ≤ Varθ(U) for every θ. Equality at θ holds exactly when U is σ(S)-measurable Pθ-almost surely.

An estimator T of a real estimand ψ is unbiased if it is integrable under every Pθ and Eθ[T] = ψ(θ) for every θ. It is finite-variance unbiased if additionally square-integrable under every Pθ. Such a T is UMVU if Varθ(T) ≤ Varθ(U) for every θ and every other finite-variance unbiased estimator U of the same estimand.

For a real measurable estimator T of ψ, Biasθ(T) = Eθ[T] − ψ(θ) when T is Pθ-integrable, and MSEθ(T) = Eθ[(T − ψ(θ))²] ∈ [0,+∞]. This MSE is the risk of the deterministic rule induced by T under squared-error loss.

For a measurable statistic T from the data measurable space to an action measurable space, K_T(x,B) = δ_{T(x)}(B) = 1_B(T(x)) is a probability kernel and therefore a deterministic randomized procedure.
For a sigma-algebra A on X, x₀ ∈ X, and every nonnegative A-measurable f:X → [0,+∞], the integral of f against δ_{x₀} equals f(x₀).
For a real estimator T with Eθ[T²] < ∞, MSEθ(T) = Varθ(T) + Biasθ(T)².

Assume AC and a standard-Borel experiment with a standard-Borel complete sufficient statistic S under the common conditional-law interface. If g is Borel and g(S) is unbiased for ψ with finite variance under every Pθ, then g(S) is UMVU, and any other UMVU estimator equals g(S) Pθ-almost surely for each θ.

seams_checked.note: Checked the page and the statistic, randomized-procedure, and action-law suppliers. The deterministic-kernel lemma preserves pointwise kernel requirements; Rao–Blackwell applies the action-law result to the common kernel as a procedure for the pushforward experiment.

The bias/MSE definition faithfully uses nonnegative, possibly infinite risk with sectionwise measurable loss. The local Dirac evaluation lemma supplies the reduction to deterministic squared-error expectation without imposing parameter measurability.

Rao–Blackwell preserves the supplied common-kernel and standard-Borel sufficiency hypotheses. Lehmann–Scheffé applies completeness only to one measurable real function of S that is integrable and has zero expectation under every parameter.

Read both Cramér–Rao carriers. They accurately describe global finite-variance unbiasedness as sufficient for their pointwise mean and moment premises, while retaining the score-covariance or score-derivative identity as a separate hypothesis. The vector use is explicitly coordinatewise.

The sparse-sequence lower-bound carrier cites the deterministic-kernel lemma in F7 and applies it to the Borel vector estimator and its first coordinate. Both have the required Borel action spaces; the cited lemma supplies precisely their admissible point-mass kernels.
